analysis.one_liner: Restores older workers' ability to prove age discrimination when age was a motivating factor, not the only cause.
analysis.headline: The bill to restore older workers' ability to sue for age discrimination died in a Senate committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2009 the Supreme Court's Gross v. FBL Financial decision made it much harder to win an age-discrimination case: a worker had to prove age was the deciding reason for being fired, demoted, or not hired, not just one reason. This bill would have changed the law back so a worker could win by showing age was a motivating factor, the same standard used for race or sex discrimination. It had a Democratic sponsor and 24 cosponsors in the Senate, got one hearing, and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers aged 40 and over who believe they were fired, demoted, or passed over because of their age. Under the Supreme Court's Gross decision, they had to prove age was the sole cause of the adverse decision; this bill would have let them win by showing age was one motivating factor, the same standard used for race or sex discrimination claims. It also would have applied to pending claims and, through its broad language, to retaliation and whistleblower claims.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers 40 and over facing age discrimination

how_it_helps.text: It would let a worker prove age discrimination by showing age was a motivating factor — even if other factors also played a part — instead of proving age was the sole deciding cause.
It would allow workers to use any admissible circumstantial or direct evidence and any established method of proving discrimination, rather than the narrower paths the Supreme Court allowed.
It would specify the relief and damages available to a successful age-discrimination plaintiff, restoring remedies the Gross decision had limited.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — private companies and governments — who would face more age-discrimination lawsuits that could survive, and could have to pay damages, reinstate workers, or cover attorney's fees when they lose. When an employer proves it would have made the same decision without the age factor, the bill limits relief to declarations and injunctions, not money damages.

drawbacks.text: The bill would make it easier to win age-discrimination suits even when other factors — including legitimate business ones — also motivated the decision, which employers argued would increase litigation and liability costs.
The bill applies retroactively to all claims pending on or after June 17, 2009, letting already-filed cases benefit from the new, easier standard.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would be restoring age-discrimination protections for workers 40 and over at a time when laid-off older workers face particular difficulty; the chief cost is to employers, who would face more lawsuits and mixed-motive claims, though the bill limits damages when the employer proves it would have acted the same way anyway. The main design weakness is not the standard itself but timing: the bill sat in committee while the Gross ruling stood, leaving a gap between protections for age claims and claims under other anti-discrimination laws.

outcome.mechanism: After a single committee hearing in May 2010, the bill went nowhere: no markup, no floor vote, and the Congress ended with it still stuck in committee.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 6, 2009 and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
The committee held one hearing on the bill on May 6, 2010, but never reported it to the full Senate.
No further action was taken before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers facing potential age-discrimination suits are better off, because the stricter standard from the Gross decision remained in place.

for.name: Tom Harkin (D-IA)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to overturn the Gross v. FBL Financial decision by restoring the motivating-factor standard for age discrimination.

for.name: 24 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 24 cosponsors were Democrats or independents.

for.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on May 6, 2010 (printed as S.Hrg. 111-1122).

against.name: Business and employer groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, arguing it would raise litigation costs for employers by making mixed-motive discrimination claims easier to win.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Held a hearing but never brought the bill to a committee vote, leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 24 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's independent; no Republicans signed on, and the bill never reached a floor vote where broader support could have been tested.

industries.note: Would face an easier legal standard for age-discrimination suits, meaning more cases could survive dismissal and more could reach juries, with the possibility of damages and reinstatement. The bill was a direct response to a ruling that had shielded employers from many such claims.

The group the bill is designed to protect: laid-off and passed-over older employees would get a realistic chance to prove age discrimination, as victims of race or sex discrimination already can under Title VII.

Would see more viable age- and retaliation-discrimination cases to bring; the bill's remedies provisions would also allow attorney's fees in some circumstances. Not a major cost to the public, but a concentrated interest that would have benefited.
